extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of natural philosophy / evolutionary theory
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook/chapter-level exposition describing the physical and biological principles by which uniform forces acting on aggregates produce differentiation and the local integration (segregation) of unlike units; includes illustrative examples from mechanics, chemistry, geology, astronomy, and anatomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE MULTIPLICATION OF EFFECTS
rubrics_metrics.description: A uniform incident force falling on a heterogeneous aggregate will be reduced into a group of multiform secondary forces; the multiplication of effects (secondary forces and transformations) is a part-cause of evolution and increases with heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as a corollary of the persistence of force: different constituent forces in parts of a whole produce different reactions to a uniform incident force, creating secondary forces that undergo further transformations. Examples are general and conceptual; no numerical scoring but presented as a fundamental principle from which other phenomena follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences known by differences in reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Things which we call different are things which react in different ways; we can know them as different only by the differences in their reactions to incident forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by hardness/softness, colour (decomposition of light), and the assertion that objective unlikeness is presence in one thing of some force(s) not present in another. Philosophical warrant tied to assuming persistence of force (otherwise changes would have no antecedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective unlikeness grounded in persistence of force
rubrics_metrics.description: When we predicate unlikeness between two objects from differing effects on consciousness, our warrant is the persistence of force — the change is ascribed to some force in one object not present in the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that denying this is equivalent to denying persistence of force. Used as foundational justification for treating observed differences as due to differing constituent forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform force on heterogeneous aggregate leads to dispersion and qualitative differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: A uniform force falling on a uniform aggregate must undergo dispersion; falling on an aggregate of unlike parts it undergoes dispersion from each part and qualitative differentiations in proportion to the unlikeness and number of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to many secondary forces that transform while producing equivalent transformations in parts; conclusion drawn both inductively and deductively from fundamental truths about forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segregation: local integration accompanies local differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: As parts of a whole become unlike (local differentiation), they also become clearly marked off and gathered into distinct groups (local integration or segregation) rather than producing vague chaotic heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduced via many concrete instances (leaves collected by wind, separation of sand/pebbles by currents, winnowing) to motivate why segregation occurs alongside differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective action of uniform forces separates components by differing attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniform forces (air, water currents, electric/magnetic attraction, chemical affinity) acting indiscriminately on mixed aggregates separate units according to size, specific gravity, solubility, magnetic properties, etc., producing segregated minor aggregates each of like units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: autumn leaves collected by wind, river deposition of boulders/sand/mud, winnowing chaff from wheat, emery separation through successive compartments, magnetized gauze separating steel-dust from stone-dust, laboratory separations of soluble/insoluble matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness of separation proportional to definiteness of difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Other things equal, the clearness (definiteness) with which mixed units separate is proportionate to how definite the differences among those units are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: a handful of fragments with gradual size differences segregates only indefinitely under breeze; distinct orders (pebbles, sand, dust) segregate more definitely. Distillation (alcohol/water) shows difficulty when units are similar; crystallization of unlike salts shows easy segregation, while isomorphous salts co-crystallize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical similarity impedes segregation (isomorphism)
rubrics_metrics.description: When salts or substances are chemically homologous or isomorphous (similar in structure and crystalline form), they tend to crystallize together and resist segregation except under special, repeated processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: nitrates or sulphates that are isomorphous unite in same crystals and will not separate by ordinary crystallization; repeated re-solution and crystallization may reduce impurities. Emphasizes that segregation ease depends on degree of unlikeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between mechanical transposition and molecular rearrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: The incident permanently effective force falling on compound parts may be expended either in modifying mutual relations of constituents (molecular/chemical rearrangements) or in moving parts (mechanical transposition); the portion not used for one must work on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If little force is absorbed in molecular changes, more will produce mechanical motion of compound units and cause segregation by movement; conversely, if mechanical transposition is minimal, molecular changes dominate. Determines whether segregation is mechanical or chemical in character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different resultant forces on like units cause segregation (action of unlike forces on like units)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a group of like units within an aggregate is exposed to forces unlike in amount or direction to those acting on the rest, that group will separate and integrate (segregate) provided some portion of the force remains effective for motion rather than being dissipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to astronomical/nebular contexts (formation of rings and planets), where differential forces during concentration cause parts to remain behind or separate; also applies generally where unequal resultant forces exist across an aggregate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed forces segregated by reaction of uniform matters (dispersion of light example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Just as uniform forces segregate mixed matters, mixed forces are segregated by reaction of uniform matters: e.g., a beam of light containing different orders of undulation is refracted differentially producing spectral colors, or absorbed differently when traversing obstructing media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: dispersion in refraction producing the colours of the spectrum; absorption of short undulations before long ones so red rays penetrate when obstruction is great; divergence produced when adjacent beams pass through unlike substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geologic segregation by currents, cooling, and post-depositional processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Geologic changes show segregation of unlike units by uniform incident forces: coastal waves and tides sort materials by particle size/density; rivers deposit materials by current strength; slow cooling of igneous masses allows segregation and crystallization (granite) while rapid cooling yields more uniform textures (basalt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: shore sorting into mud/sand/pebbles/boulders; flints and iron-pyrite nodules formed by local aggregation during deposition; bog iron; deposition of volcanic sublimates at different crevices; granite crystal size variation in dykes reflecting cooling rates and mobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological/organismic segregation driven by mechanical strains and functional unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Within organisms, segregation (coalescence or retention of separate units) corresponds to the uniformity or variety of incident forces due to function: parts exposed to common strains coalesce; parts exposed to differing forces remain separate or become distinct segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: vertebral column shows integration corresponding to unity of incident forces with segmentation reflecting variety of forces; sacrum vertebrae fuse where common strain transmits body weight; metacarpals coalesce into cannon bones in ungulates where separate toe movements are absent; Olyptodon dermal armour led to vertebral fusion due to uniform pressure and prevention of relative movement.
